question: A 59-year-old woman with a personal history of breast cancer operated on 8 months ago and osteoporosis, suffers a fall and has a fracture of the right femur neck. She is operated on surgically and remains in bed with plaster for 10 days. A week after her high note suddenly a shortness of breath that leads her to consult her GP who notes that her right calf has edema and pain on palpation. What clinical elements would NOT be important in determining that you have a high clinical risk of pulmonary thromboembolism ?:

options.opc: The antecedent of having been more than 3 days at rest.
options.opd: The presence of unilateral edema of the right calf.

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "History of breast cancer" -> "increased risk of thromboembolic events" -> "potentially relevant for pulmonary thromboembolism" -> 85%
CHAIN: "History of osteoporosis" -> "not directly related to thromboembolic risk" -> "less relevant for pulmonary thromboembolism" -> 70%
CHAIN: "Antecedent of being more than 3 days at rest" -> "increased risk of venous stasis" -> "high clinical risk of pulmonary thromboembolism" -> 90%
CHAIN: "Presence of unilateral edema of the right calf" -> "suggestive of deep vein thrombosis" -> "high clinical risk of pulmonary thromboembolism" -> 95%
enhanced_information: In assessing the clinical risk of pulmonary thromboembolism (PE) in this patient, the following points are relevant: 1. The history of breast cancer is associated with an increased risk of thromboembolic events, making it relevant for PE risk assessment. 2. The history of osteoporosis does not directly correlate with an increased risk of thromboembolism, thus it is less relevant in this context. 3. Being more than 3 days at rest significantly increases the risk of venous stasis, which is a major risk factor for PE. 4. The presence of unilateral edema in the right calf is suggestive of deep vein thrombosis (DVT), which is a precursor to PE. Therefore, the history of osteoporosis (option opb) would NOT be important in determining a high clinical risk of pulmonary thromboembolism.
analysis: In assessing the risk of pulmonary thromboembolism (PE), certain clinical elements are more relevant than others. The history of breast cancer (opa) is significant as it is a known risk factor for thromboembolic events. The history of osteoporosis (opb) is less directly related to PE risk, although it can be associated with thrombosis. The antecedent of being more than 3 days at rest (opc) is crucial, as prolonged immobility is a well-established risk factor for venous thromboembolism. The presence of unilateral edema of the right calf (opd) is also a classic sign of deep vein thrombosis (DVT), which can lead to PE. Therefore, the history of osteoporosis is the least relevant in determining a high clinical risk of pulmonary thromboembolism compared to the other options.
